newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to blast corruption in radio address.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to blast corruption in radio address.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin will fire a new salvo against corruption in a regular radio address early on Thursday (0500 GMT).

Details of the speech, which the Kremlin said was recorded on Wednesday, were not known. But Yeltsin may flesh out plans for a number of anti-corruption decrees which ministers have said will be promulgated very shortly.
The 66-year-old president has made fighting corruption a central theme of his political comeback of the past couple of months after his long illness.

In a state of the nation address on March 6, which paved the way for a sweeping government reshuffle that brought in or promoted a number of youthful liberals, he depicted Russian society as stagnating in a web of bureaucratic red tape and graft that was turning people against his free market reforms.

On Wednesday, in a soundbite replayed throughout the day across the nation's television networks, Yeltsin told his liberal new First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov that all officials should follow their honest example.

"You and I have the same credo -- not to take bribes," Yeltsin said. "He hasn't taken a kopeck and I haven't taken a kopeck," he added, referring to the subdivision of the rouble rendered obsolete by rampant hyperinflation in recent years.
Economy Minister Yakov Urinson, another of the liberal risers in the new government, said Yeltsin had already signed a decree aimed at reducing corruption on Tuesday.
"By this presidential decree... we are closing all the main channels for abuse in this area," he told Ekho Moskvy radio.
Nemtsov, 37, is to chair a meeting on Saturday that will seek to pin down details of a decree aimed at ensuring that federal contracts are filled by fair and open tender.
Sweetheart deals with federal contractors are seen as a major source of illicit income for some officials.

Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Kulikov, who is also Interior Minister and has a brief to stamp out economic crime, was quoted as saying that the decree "On Immediate Measures to Prevent Corruption" was just a partial step and a much wider document was being worked on by legal and security agencies.
Few Russians believe the administration can root out the graft that has plagued officialdom since tsarist times.
As Economy Minister Urinson observed: "Total 100 percent prevention is impossible because our people are very inventive."
Yeltsin will also speak about strengthening the state's authority in his radio address, the Kremlin said.
He seems keen to show a firm hand, both to his communist opponents in parliament and to the goverment, before leaving for a spring holiday after an official visit to Germany next week.

On Wednesday, he accused the communist-dominated lower house of overstepping the constitution, saying in a letter to its speaker Gennady Seleznyov that it had no right to make political judgements on foreign and domestic policy.
He also had strong words for the upper house, the Federation Council, where the communist lobby has been reinforced by recent local elections.
"We will work together, as long as you take into account that I am the head of state," Yeltsin was quoted as saying.
